Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: extend the data-retention job to cover the tables that have appeared since it was written, and close a gap the privacy policy currently has to admit.

## Read first
`lib/retention.ts` and `docs/retention.md`. The existing job has four rules, a `--dry-run` default, batched deletes, and a `NEVER_PRUNED` list. **Match its design exactly** — same structure, same discipline of naming a reader before pruning anything, same honesty about what it gives up.

## The tables it does not yet cover
Every one of these was added after that job was written, and several accumulate on hot paths:

- **`FormSubmission`** — public, unauthenticated writes from published sites. The agent that built it explicitly flagged that a retention rule is needed and that the policy judgement was not theirs to make. Note `spam: true` rows are kept deliberately so a false positive is recoverable and the rate is measurable — decide whether they should age out faster than real ones, and justify it.
- **`AdminAuditLog`** — an accountability record. **Think hard before pruning this at all.** A short retention on an audit log defeats its purpose; too long and it is a growing store of who-looked-at-whose-account. One measurement to weigh: a short browsing session generated 144 rows, because `site.viewed` records every render.
- **`ModerationFinding`** — evidence about abuse. Reviewed and unreviewed rows are not the same thing.
- **`EmailLog`** — the idempotency guard for transactional email. **Pruning this can cause a DUPLICATE SEND.** Read how `dedupeKey` works before touching it, and if the safe retention is "never", say so.
- **`LoginAttempt`** — already self-prunes inside `lib/rate-limit.ts`; the author argued deliberately that it does not belong in `retention.ts`. **Read that reasoning and either agree or rebut it** — do not silently duplicate the pruning, which would be worse than either choice.
- **`Event`** — already has a rule at 400 days. Re-check whether it still holds now that ratings and follow-up intents are stored there.

## Method — the part that matters
For each table: **find who reads it before you propose pruning it.** The existing job refused to prune `Build` rows and `Build.prompt` on exactly that basis, and it was right. Grep for the readers, name them in a comment, and where a reader would be affected say so rather than quietly accepting the loss.

Where the honest answer is "never prune this", say that and put it in `NEVER_PRUNED` with the reasoning.

## Also update `docs/retention.md`
It is the document the privacy policy quotes. `app/legal/privacy/page.tsx` currently has to say some data is retained indefinitely — your rules are what let that become a real commitment, so the doc must state each period plainly enough to quote.

## Scope — ONLY: `lib/retention.ts`, `scripts/retention.mjs`, `docs/retention.md`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, any other lib file, app/**, .env, package.json, other docs.

## Constraints
- **`--dry-run` stays the default.** Deleting requires `--apply`. Never weaken that.
- **Do not prune `CreditLedger`.** It is an auditable financial record, it is what stops reward-credit farming across account deletions, and it carries the Stripe payment record.
- Deletes must stay batched and bounded.
- Test in dry-run against the local database. If you want to prove a delete path, create your own throwaway rows and remove them. **Do not `--apply` against data you did not create** — note that command has been blocked by the permission system before, so plan around needing dry-run plus seeded fixtures.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0 errors, 0 warnings, 209 tests.**

## Report back
Each table with its proposed period and the reader you checked, anything you refused to prune and why, your verdict on the `LoginAttempt` question, the `EmailLog` duplicate-send risk, and dry-run counts against the real database.

1	# Kodely data retention policy
2	
3	Owner: Kodely operator (single-operator today).
4	
5	This is the document a privacy policy can quote. Every number in it is
6	enforced by code, not by intention: the policy lives in `lib/retention.ts` and
7	is executed by `scripts/retention.mjs`. If the two ever disagree with this
8	page, the code is right and this page is stale — fix it.
9	
10	Board context: before this existed there was no pruning, cron or retention job
11	anywhere in the repo, which meant the only honest thing a privacy policy could
12	say about any of this data was "retained indefinitely."
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 1. What we keep, and for how long
17	
18	| Data | Retained | Enforced by |
19	| --- | --- | --- |
20	| Sign-in sessions | Deleted as soon as they expire (30 days) | `sessions` |
21	| Rollback snapshots of your site | The 20 most recent checkpoints per project, always at least 30 days | `build-snapshots` |
22	| Product analytics events | About 13 months (400 days) | `events` |
23	| Stripe webhook receipts | 12 months (365 days) | `stripe-events` |
24	| Your projects, files, chat and build history | Until **you** delete them | — (never on a timer) |
25	| Credit ledger | Permanently | — (never pruned) |
26	
27	### Plain-language version, for a privacy policy
28	
29	> **Sessions.** We delete expired sign-in sessions immediately. A session
30	> lasts 30 days.
31	>
32	> **Site checkpoints.** Every successful build saves a full copy of your
33	> site so you can roll back to it. We keep the 20 most recent checkpoints for
34	> each project, and never remove a checkpoint less than 30 days old. Older
35	> checkpoints beyond that depth are removed; the build history entry stays.
36	>
37	> **Analytics.** We keep a record of product actions (signed up, created a
38	> project, build started, build succeeded, published) for about 13 months, and
39	> then delete it. These records contain no prompt text and no generated
40	> content.
41	>
42	> **Payments.** We keep a receipt of each processed payment notification for
43	> 12 months. Your credit ledger — every credit granted, spent or refunded — is
44	> a financial record and is kept permanently.
45	>
46	> **Your work.** Your projects, files, messages and build history are kept for
47	> as long as you keep them. Deleting a project deletes them; deleting your
48	> account deletes all of them. Neither is on a timer, and neither can be
49	> undone.
50	>
51	> **Account deletion.** Your analytics events are detached from your account
52	> immediately (the user id is removed, and cannot be re-attached), and the rows
53	> themselves are deleted within 400 days under the rule above.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## 2. Why each number
58	
59	Full reasoning, including the readers that were checked, is in the comments in
60	`lib/retention.ts`. Short version:
61	
62	**Expired sessions — deleted immediately, no grace period.**
63	`lib/auth.ts` already refuses an expired session at read time, so the row has
64	no remaining function. What it still has is a user id in a table forever.
65	Keeping data whose only surviving property is "could be breached" is pure
66	liability.
67	
68	**Rollback snapshots — newest 20 per project, floor of 30 days.**
69	`Build.filesSnapshot` is a full JSON copy of the source tree *and* the compiled
70	build output, written after every successful build. It is by far the largest
71	thing the database stores: on the development database, real snapshots measure
72	about **105 kB each after compression** — roughly one fifth of the entire
73	`ProjectFile` table per single build.
74	
75	Nothing in the product caps how far back restore reaches
76	(`app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts` lists every successful build with no
77	limit), so there was no existing depth to copy and 20 is a judgement call made
78	deliberately deep. Rollback is used to undo the last few edits. The 30-day
79	floor exists so that someone iterating hard for an afternoon — who can bury a
80	checkpoint past rank 20 within hours — never loses rollback mid-session.
81	
82	**Analytics events — 400 days.**
83	The product does not need this. Every aggregate reader in `lib/events.ts`
84	(`activationFunnel`, `greenBuildRate`, `followUpIntents`, `buildRatings`) takes
85	a window, and every caller in `app/admin` passes **30 days**. 400 days exists
86	purely so year-over-year comparison stays possible: 365 days plus a month of
87	reporting slack, which is the shortest window that still answers "how does this
88	August compare to last August".
89	
90	**Stripe webhook receipts — 365 days.**
91	`StripeEvent` rows exist only to dedupe webhook redeliveries — the billing
92	webhook inserts one *before* granting credits and relies on the unique-key
93	conflict. Stripe abandons automatic retries within about 3 days, so a year is
94	roughly a hundredfold margin. Residual risk, stated plainly: a **manual**
95	resend from the Stripe dashboard of an event older than a year would no longer
96	be deduped and could grant credits twice. A year-old manual resend warrants a
97	human look regardless.

101	## 3. What is deliberately never deleted
102	
103	**`CreditLedger` — permanently retained. Never prune this.**
104	It is an auditable financial record. The credit balance is *derived* from the
105	ledger rather than stored as a counter, so removing any row rewrites history
106	and can change a live balance. It survives project deletion by design
107	(`buildId` becomes null, the row stays).
108	
109	**`Build` rows.** Only the `filesSnapshot` column is ever cleared; the row
110	itself stays for the life of the project. Two readers make deletion unsafe:
111	the admin overview and the admin user page both aggregate `costMicros` and
112	`creditsCharged` over *all* builds for lifetime unit economics, and
113	`CreditLedger.buildId` points at builds with `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so deleting
114	builds silently detaches spend from the thing that caused it.
115	
116	**`Build.prompt`.** Free text the user wrote, and therefore a tempting
117	redaction target — but it is the visible label of every checkpoint in the
118	history panel. Redacting old prompts would turn old checkpoints into
119	unlabelled rows. It lives and dies with the project.
120	
121	**`ProjectFile`, `Message`, `Project`.** The user's actual work. Deleted when
122	the user deletes the project or the account, never on a timer.

126	## 4. Running it
127	
128	```bash
129	node scripts/retention.mjs                    # dry run — the default
130	node scripts/retention.mjs --only events      # dry run, one rule
131	node scripts/retention.mjs --apply            # actually delete
132	```
133	
134	`--dry-run` is the default and needs no flag; **deleting requires typing
135	`--apply`.** Counting and deleting are separate functions in
136	`lib/retention.ts` — the counting path issues SELECTs only and physically
137	cannot delete — so the dry-run table is trustworthy rather than a
138	`if (dryRun)` branch away from the real thing.
139	
140	Deletes are batched (500 rows per statement) and each pass re-runs its
141	selection instead of paging by offset, so the job never holds a long lock and
142	can be interrupted and resumed safely.
143	
144	`DATABASE_URL` is read from `.env` by the same parser the eval harness uses
145	(`scripts/eval/loader.mjs`). The run prints the host and database name it is
146	about to touch — check it before typing `--apply`.
147	
148	### Scheduling
149	
150	Nothing schedules this today: `deploy.sh` deploys and restarts the service and
151	sets up no timers. Add a cron entry on the VM as the `kodely` user (prod lives
152	at `/opt/kodely`):
153	
154	```cron
155	# Kodely data retention — 04:15 daily, off-peak. Logs kept for post-hoc review.
156	15 4 * * * cd /opt/kodely && /usr/bin/node scripts/retention.mjs --apply >> /var/log/kodely-retention.log 2>&1
157	```
158	
159	Two notes on operating it:
160	
161	- **Do the first run by hand, without `--apply`**, and read the table. The
162	  first enforcement after a long unpruned period is the largest one this job
163	  will ever do.
164	- **Postgres does not return freed space to the filesystem.** Deleted rows go
165	  onto each table's free list and are reused; autovacuum reclaims them in the
166	  background. If disk needs to come back immediately, `VACUUM` the affected
167	  tables by hand. `VACUUM FULL` rewrites and takes an exclusive lock — do not
168	  run it casually on a live database.

164	export function daysAgo(days: number): Date {
165	  return new Date(Date.now() - days * 86_400_000);

168	/**
169	 * Total on-disk size of a table including its indexes and TOAST. Used to turn
170	 * a row count into a byte estimate proportionally, which is cheap and — unlike
171	 * summing row widths — accounts for the index entries that also go away.
172	 */
173	async function relationBytes(table: string): Promise<number | null> {
174	  const rows = await db.$queryRaw<{ size: bigint | null }[]>`
175	    SELECT pg_total_relation_size(${`"${table}"`}::regclass) AS size`;
176	  const size = rows[0]?.size;
177	  return size == null ? null : Number(size);
178	}
179	
180	/** Proportional byte estimate: whole-table size scaled by the share going away. */
181	async function estimateBytes(table: string, rows: number, total: number): Promise<number | null> {
182	  if (rows === 0) return 0;
183	  if (total === 0) return null;
184	  const size = await relationBytes(table);
185	  return size === null ? null : Math.round((size * rows) / total);
186	}

188	/**
189	 * The one batched-mutation loop, shared by every rule.
190	 *
191	 * `selectIds` hands back at most `take` ids that still match the rule, and
192	 * `mutate` removes them. Each pass re-runs the selection rather than paging
193	 * with an offset, so rows the previous pass handled drop out of the candidate
194	 * set naturally and concurrent inserts cannot shift a window underneath us.
195	 */
196	async function purgeInBatches(
197	  selectIds: (take: number) => Promise<string[]>,
198	  mutate: (ids: string[]) => Promise<number>,
199	): Promise<RetentionPurge> {
200	  let rows = 0;
201	  let batches = 0;
202	
203	  while (batches < MAX_BATCHES) {
204	    const ids = await selectIds(BATCH_SIZE);
205	    if (ids.length === 0) return { rows, batches, truncated: false };
206	
207	    const affected = await mutate(ids);
208	    batches++;
209	    rows += affected;
210	
211	    // Selected rows but changed none: the mutation is not narrowing the
212	    // candidate set, so the next pass would select the same ids forever.
213	    if (affected === 0) return { rows, batches, truncated: true };
214	  }
215	
216	  return { rows, batches, truncated: true };
217	}

4	// Credits already cap spend per build, but nothing stops a broken or
5	// malicious client from firing many rapid requests before a human notices —
6	// and a free, unmetered *.kodely.site subdomain is a spam/phishing vector
7	// independent of credit spend. These are coarse, cheap safety nets, not a
8	// content-moderation system (there is no classifier here — a page can still
9	// be abusive content and pass both checks; that's a separate, harder problem
10	// left for a dedicated moderation pass, not faked here with a weak heuristic).
11	
12	const GENERATE_LIMIT = 20; // per user, per rolling hour
13	const PUBLISH_LIMIT = 15; // new (first-time) publishes per user, per rolling day
14	const ENHANCE_LIMIT = 40; // per user, per rolling hour
15	
16	export async function checkGenerateRateLimit(
17	  userId: string,
18	): Promise<{ allowed: boolean; retryAfterSeconds?: number }> {
19	  const since = new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60_000);
20	  const count = await db.build.count({
21	    where: { project: { userId }, createdAt: { gte: since } },
22	  });
23	  if (count < GENERATE_LIMIT) return { allowed: true };
24	  return { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds: 3600 };
25	}
26	
27	export async function checkPublishRateLimit(
28	  userId: string,
29	): Promise<{ allowed: boolean; retryAfterSeconds?: number }> {
30	  const since = new Date(Date.now() - 24 * 60 * 60_000);
31	  // Counts DISTINCT projects touched by a publish in the window, not publish
32	  // events — republishing the same project repeatedly still counts once.
33	  // That's the right shape: the abuse case is many distinct spam subdomains,
34	  // not heavy iteration on one real site (which credits already gate).
35	  const count = await db.project.count({
36	    where: { userId, publishedAt: { gte: since } },
37	  });
38	  if (count < PUBLISH_LIMIT) return { allowed: true };
39	  return { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds: 86_400 };
40	}

42	// In memory, and synchronous, unlike the two checks above — an enhance leaves
43	// nothing in the database to count. It writes no files, creates no build row
44	// and charges no credits by design (see lib/enhance.ts), and a throwaway
45	// suggestion does not justify its own table. So this is per-process and resets
46	// on every deploy: a speed bump, exactly like the contact form's throttle, and
47	// the right weight for a call that costs a fraction of a cent. The real
48	// spending gate is still checkGenerateRateLimit plus the credit meter — those
49	// sit in front of the only thing here that costs real money.
50	//
51	// The ceiling is deliberately well above checkGenerateRateLimit's 20 builds an
52	// hour: enhancing several drafts before committing to one build is the whole
53	// point of the feature, and a limit that punished that would fight it.
54	const enhanceHits = new Map<string, number[]>();
55	
56	export function checkEnhanceRateLimit(userId: string): {
57	  allowed: boolean;
58	  retryAfterSeconds?: number;
59	} {
60	  const now = Date.now();
61	  const cutoff = now - 60 * 60_000;
62	  const recent = (enhanceHits.get(userId) ?? []).filter((t) => t > cutoff);
63	
64	  // Bound the map so a long-lived process can't accumulate one entry per user
65	  // forever. Clearing wholesale (rather than evicting) briefly resets everyone
66	  // — acceptable for a speed bump, and it never denies a legitimate request.
67	  if (enhanceHits.size > 5000) enhanceHits.clear();
68	
69	  if (recent.length >= ENHANCE_LIMIT) {
70	    enhanceHits.set(userId, recent);
71	    // Wait until the oldest hit in the window ages out, not a flat hour.
72	    return {
73	      allowed: false,
74	      retryAfterSeconds: Math.max(1, Math.ceil((recent[0] - cutoff) / 1000)),
75	    };
76	  }
77	
78	  recent.push(now);
79	  enhanceHits.set(userId, recent);
80	  return { allowed: true };

83	// ===========================================================================
84	// PRE-AUTH limiting (login / signup)
85	// ===========================================================================
86	//
87	// Everything above keys on `userId`, so none of it can run before a session
88	// exists. Login and signup are the two routes that are reachable by anyone and
89	// that are worth attacking: unlimited password guessing on one side, and on the
90	// other a free account that is immediately granted SIGNUP_GRANT credits — real
91	// model spend, minted by a POST.
92	//
93	// STORAGE: the `LoginAttempt` table. One row per attempt that was actually
94	// charged to a bucket, `(scope, key, createdAt)`, where `key` is a client IP or
95	// a salted digest of an email and never a plaintext address. Rows live at most
96	// as long as the longest rule window (a day) — see the prune below.
97	//
98	// WHY THE TABLE IS NOT READ ON THE REQUEST PATH. Prisma is async, and the two
99	// gates below are synchronous — `app/api/auth/login/route.ts` calls
100	// `checkLoginRateLimit(req, email)` without awaiting it, and it must stay that
101	// way, both because a route change is out of scope and because a synchronous
102	// check is what closes the concurrency hole documented on that function. So the
103	// shape here is a DURABLE LEDGER (LoginAttempt) with an in-process INDEX over
104	// the live window in front of it:
105	//
106	//   * a verdict is computed from the in-process index — no query, no await;
107	//   * a consumed attempt is appended to the index synchronously AND queued as
108	//     one INSERT (queued, never awaited, so the request never waits on it);
109	//   * every RECONCILE_MS the index is rebuilt from the table, which is also how
110	//     it is populated in the first place after a restart. The two login scopes
111	//     are rebuilt on every tick; the slow-moving signup scope every
112	//     FULL_RECONCILE_MS, because it is the one that costs anything to read.
113	//
114	// That is the whole point of the change: the counters are no longer lost when
115	// the process restarts, because the process's memory is a cache of the table
116	// rather than the only copy. Two consequences worth stating plainly:
117	//
118	//   * MULTI-PROCESS: no longer multiplies by the process count, but it does not
119	//     compose instantly either — two processes converge within RECONCILE_MS on
120	//     the login scopes and FULL_RECONCILE_MS on signup. A cluster gets a limit
121	//     that is off by at most one interval of traffic per extra process, instead
122	//     of one that is off by a factor of N. It is still worth saying that a
123	//     shared in-memory store (Redis) is the answer if this ever becomes a real
124	//     cluster; this makes N processes tolerable, not correct.
125	//   * COLD START: the index is empty until the first reconcile finishes, and a
126	//     verdict computed from an empty index would be the fail-open behaviour
127	//     this change exists to remove. So the gates fail CLOSED until then — see
128	//     `hydrated` below. That is one 429 with `Retry-After: 1` per process
129	//     lifetime, not one per user.
130	//
131	// WRITE VOLUME under attack is bounded by the limits themselves, not by request
132	// rate: a blocked attempt returns before `record`, so it writes nothing at all.
133	// Once an attacker trips a bucket every further guess from them is a pure
134	// in-memory comparison. The only DB work that scales with anything is the
135	// reconcile — a fixed one or two queries per interval per process, whatever the
136	// request rate — and the prune, which runs on the same timer.
137	//
138	// FAIL DIRECTION: closed. A request whose client IP cannot be established (see
139	// clientIp) is not waved through — it lands in one shared, strict bucket. Same
140	// answer for a database outage: both auth routes read the same Postgres this

143	// turn any DB blip into an unlimited-guessing window.

145	/**
146	 * The client's IP, as the key for a pre-auth bucket.
147	 *
148	 * WHICH HEADER, AND WHY IT MATTERS: this app sits behind Cloudflare → host
149	 * nginx → VM nginx, so the socket peer is always a proxy and the address has to
150	 * come from a header. Only ONE header here is trustworthy:
151	 *
152	 *  * `cf-connecting-ip` — SET by Cloudflare on every request, overwriting
153	 *    whatever the client sent. A client cannot forge it through the edge. This
154	 *    is the one we use.
155	 *  * `x-forwarded-for` FIRST entry — ATTACKER-CONTROLLED. Cloudflare *appends*
156	 *    to any XFF the client supplied rather than replacing it, so entry 0 is

158	 *    fresh bucket per request and the limiter does nothing. (That is exactly
159	 *    finding M3 against app/api/contact/route.ts, which is why this file does
160	 *    not repeat it.)
161	 *  * `x-forwarded-for` LAST entry — useless here, though not spoofable. Each
162	 *    nginx hop appends the address of the hop *before* it, so the last entry on
163	 *    arrival is our own front nginx, a constant. Keying on it would put every
164	 *    visitor on the planet in one bucket.

166	 * NO `cf-connecting-ip` ⇒ the request did not come through the edge (local dev,
167	 * a health check, or someone hitting the origin IP directly). Next gives a route
168	 * handler no socket address to fall back on, so all such traffic shares one
169	 * bucket named below. That is deliberate and fails closed: direct-to-origin
170	 * traffic is throttled as a single collective client rather than being exempt.
171	 *
172	 * RESIDUAL, for the record: an attacker who can reach the origin IP directly,
173	 * bypassing Cloudflare, CAN forge `cf-connecting-ip` — no application code can
174	 * detect that. The fix is at the edge, not here: restrict the origin's firewall
175	 * to Cloudflare's published ranges (or use an authenticated origin pull). That
176	 * is infrastructure work outside this repo and it is not done as far as this
177	 * checkout can tell.
178	 *
179	 * IP is also imperfect in the other direction, and knowingly so: a NAT'd office
180	 * or a carrier-grade NAT presents hundreds of real people as one key. The limits
181	 * below are sized with that in mind, and login refunds successful attempts
182	 * (see noteLoginSuccess) precisely so a busy shared address is not spent by
183	 * people who typed their password correctly.
184	 */
185	function clientIp(req: Request): string {
186	  const cf = req.headers.get("cf-connecting-ip")?.trim();
187	  if (cf) return cf.toLowerCase();
188	  return "no-edge";

191	// Emails are hashed before they are used as a bucket key. The table would
192	// otherwise be a running plaintext list of every address anyone tried to sign in
193	// as — including typos and addresses that have no account — which is a pile of
194	// personal data this feature has no reason to hold. The IP scopes store the
195	// address itself, which the schema's key contract allows and which is no more
196	// than any access log keeps, and for less time: nothing here outlives a day.
197	//
198	// THE SALT MUST BE STABLE ACROSS RESTARTS, which is the one thing that changed
199	// when this became durable. It used to be `randomBytes(16)` per process; with a
200	// durable bucket that would hand every account a brand-new, empty bucket on
201	// every deploy — precisely the failure this change exists to remove — so it is
202	// a constant instead. Set LOGIN_KEY_SALT to a secret to upgrade the digest from
203	// "a pseudonym anyone holding the source can recompute" to one that also needs
204	// the secret. Rotating it resets every account bucket exactly once, which is
205	// harmless: the windows are fifteen minutes and an hour.
206	const EMAIL_KEY_SALT = process.env.LOGIN_KEY_SALT ?? "kodely:login-attempt:v1";
207	function emailKey(email: string): string {
208	  return createHash("sha256").update(`${EMAIL_KEY_SALT}:${email.trim().toLowerCase()}`).digest("hex");

210	
211	type Rule = { limit: number; windowMs: number };
212	type Verdict = { allowed: boolean; retryAfterSeconds?: number };
213	
214	/** Matches LoginAttempt.scope. One table, three independent buckets. */
215	type Scope = "ip" | "account" | "signup";
216	
217	/**
218	 * One consumed attempt. `id` is the LoginAttempt primary key.
219	 *
220	 * `settledAt` is when this process last knew the row to be committed — the
221	 * moment its INSERT resolved, or, for a hit read back out of the table, the row
222	 * timestamp itself. It stays undefined while the INSERT is still queued or in
223	 * flight, and if the INSERT fails it stays undefined for good. A reconcile uses
224	 * it to tell "the read has not caught up with me yet" (keep the hit) from "the
225	 * read is authoritative and this row is gone" (drop it) — see `reconcile`.
226	 */
227	type Hit = { id: string; at: number; settledAt?: number };
228	
229	type Store = { scope: Scope; rules: Rule[]; hits: Map<string, Hit[]> };
230	
231	const MINUTE = 60_000;
232	const HOUR = 60 * MINUTE;
233	const DAY = 24 * HOUR;
234	
235	// Two windows per bucket rather than one: a short window stops a burst, and a
236	// long one stops a patient attacker who paces themselves just under it.
237	const LOGIN_IP_RULES: Rule[] = [
238	  { limit: 20, windowMs: 15 * MINUTE },
239	  { limit: 60, windowMs: HOUR },
240	];
241	
242	// Per ACCOUNT, across every source address. This is the rule that actually
243	// answers credential stuffing, where the whole point is that each guess arrives
244	// from a different IP. Tighter than the per-IP rule because a single account
245	// legitimately sees very few failures.
246	//
247	// The tradeoff is real and is chosen with eyes open: anyone can burn a victim's
248	// account bucket on purpose and cost them a login for a few minutes. That is
249	// why this is a ROLLING WINDOW that heals by itself, never a sticky lockout
250	// flag, and why a correct password clears it immediately — the victim's next
251	// attempt after the window slides succeeds, and no operator action is needed.
252	// An indefinite lockout would trade password guessing for a denial-of-service
253	// against any account whose email address is known.
254	const LOGIN_EMAIL_RULES: Rule[] = [
255	  { limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * MINUTE },
256	  { limit: 20, windowMs: HOUR },
257	];
258	
259	// Signup is a volume problem, not a guessing problem: one source minting many
260	// accounts. Every account that lands costs SIGNUP_GRANT credits of real model
261	// spend, so the daily rule is the one that bounds the money.
262	//
263	// Sized to be invisible to humans and to a shared office address (five accounts
264	// an hour from one IP is already an odd thing for real people to do) while
265	// capping what a single address can mint per day. A distributed botnet still
266	// gets one bucket per address — no IP-keyed limiter can fix that, and the
267	// answers to it are email verification before the grant lands, or deferring the
268	// grant until first build. Both are outside this file.
269	const SIGNUP_IP_RULES: Rule[] = [
270	  { limit: 5, windowMs: HOUR },
271	  { limit: 15, windowMs: DAY },
272	];
273	
274	const loginIp: Store = { scope: "ip", rules: LOGIN_IP_RULES, hits: new Map() };
275	const loginAccount: Store = { scope: "account", rules: LOGIN_EMAIL_RULES, hits: new Map() };
276	const signupIp: Store = { scope: "signup", rules: SIGNUP_IP_RULES, hits: new Map() };
277	const STORES: Store[] = [loginIp, loginAccount, signupIp];
278	const STORE_BY_SCOPE = new Map<string, Store>(STORES.map((s) => [s.scope, s]));
279	
280	// Ceiling on distinct keys per store, so a flood of unique addresses cannot
281	// grow memory without bound.
282	const MAX_KEYS = 20_000;
283	
284	function longestWindow(rules: Rule[]): number {
285	  return Math.max(...rules.map((r) => r.windowMs));
286	}
287	
288	function highestLimit(rules: Rule[]): number {
289	  return Math.max(...rules.map((r) => r.limit));
290	}
291	
292	/** The longest window any rule uses. Nothing older can affect any verdict. */
293	const MAX_WINDOW = Math.max(...STORES.map((s) => longestWindow(s.rules)));
294	
295	/**
296	 * Keep a store under MAX_KEYS.
297	 *
298	 * NOTE the difference from checkEnhanceRateLimit above, which clears wholesale
299	 * when it grows too large. That is fine for a speed bump on an authenticated
300	 * route; here it would be a vulnerability — an attacker could flood unique keys
301	 * to force a clear and wipe the very counter that is throttling them. So this
302	 * only ever drops entries that are already expired, and if that is not enough,
303	 * evicts the LEAST recently active first. An attacker's own bucket is by
304	 * definition the most recently active, so it is the last thing to go.
305	 *
306	 * Eviction is a memory decision only, never a durability one: the rows stay in
307	 * LoginAttempt, so an evicted key comes back at the next reconcile with its
308	 * count intact.
309	 */
310	function sweep(store: Store, now: number): void {
311	  if (store.hits.size <= MAX_KEYS) return;
312	  const windowMs = longestWindow(store.rules);
313	
314	  for (const [key, hits] of store.hits) {
315	    if (hits.length === 0 || hits[hits.length - 1].at <= now - windowMs) store.hits.delete(key);
316	  }
317	  if (store.hits.size <= MAX_KEYS) return;
318	
319	  const byLastSeen = [...store.hits.entries()].sort(
320	    (a, b) => a[1][a[1].length - 1].at - b[1][b[1].length - 1].at,
321	  );
322	  for (const [key] of byLastSeen.slice(0, store.hits.size - MAX_KEYS)) store.hits.delete(key);
323	}
324	
325	/** Read-only: would one more hit on this key breach any of its rules? */
326	function check(store: Store, key: string): Verdict {
327	  const now = Date.now();
328	  const rules = store.rules;
329	  const hits = (store.hits.get(key) ?? []).filter((h) => h.at > now - longestWindow(rules));
330	
331	  let retryAfterSeconds = 0;
332	  for (const rule of rules) {
333	    const inWindow = hits.filter((h) => h.at > now - rule.windowMs);
334	    if (inWindow.length < rule.limit) continue;
335	    // Wait only until enough hits age out of THIS window, not a flat period.
336	    const binding = inWindow[inWindow.length - rule.limit];
337	    retryAfterSeconds = Math.max(
338	      retryAfterSeconds,
339	      Math.max(1, Math.ceil((binding.at + rule.windowMs - now) / 1000)),
340	    );
341	  }
342	
343	  return retryAfterSeconds > 0 ? { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds } : { allowed: true };
344	}
345	
346	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
347	// Durable side: one serialised write queue, plus tombstones
348	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
349	
350	/**
351	 * Every mutation is queued here and never awaited by a request.
352	 *
353	 * SERIALISED, not merely fire-and-forget, and that ordering is load-bearing:
354	 * `refund` deletes the row that `record` inserts, and if the DELETE could
355	 * overtake the INSERT the row would survive and the refund would silently do
356	 * nothing. One chain guarantees the two run in call order. The chain never
357	 * rejects — a failed write is dropped, because the alternative (throwing into a
358	 * request that has already been answered) helps nobody, and the next reconcile
359	 * re-reads whatever actually landed.
360	 */
361	let writes: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve();
362	function enqueueWrite(run: () => Promise<unknown>): void {
363	  writes = writes.then(() => run().catch(() => undefined));
364	}
365	
366	/**
367	 * Rows we have deleted (or are about to) whose DELETE may not have committed
368	 * before an in-flight reconcile read them. Without this a refund could be
369	 * undone by a read that started a moment earlier. Id ⇒ expiry.
370	 */
371	const tombstones = new Map<string, number>();
372	/** Buckets cleared by a successful login. `scope\0key` ⇒ the moment of clearing. */
373	const cleared = new Map<string, number>();
374	const TOMBSTONE_MS = 60_000;
375	
376	function bucketId(scope: Scope, key: string): string {
377	  return `${scope}:${key}`;
378	}
379	
380	/**
381	 * Consume one hit: append to the index synchronously, queue the row.
382	 *
383	 * `createdAt` is set from this process's clock rather than left to the database
384	 * default, so that a row and the in-memory hit it mirrors carry the SAME
385	 * timestamp. `check` measures every window against `Date.now()`, and letting the
386	 * two clocks disagree would move hits across a window edge at each reconcile.
387	 */
388	function record(store: Store, key: string): void {
389	  const now = Date.now();
390	  sweep(store, now);
391	  const hits = (store.hits.get(key) ?? []).filter((h) => h.at > now - longestWindow(store.rules));
392	  const hit: Hit = { id: randomUUID(), at: now };
393	  hits.push(hit);
394	  store.hits.set(key, hits);
395	
396	  const scope = store.scope;
397	  enqueueWrite(async () => {
398	    await db.loginAttempt.create({ data: { id: hit.id, key, scope, createdAt: new Date(hit.at) } });
399	    hit.settledAt = Date.now();
400	  });
401	}
402	
403	/**
404	 * Give back the single most recent hit on a key.
405	 *
406	 * WHY A DELETE, AND NOT A COMPENSATING ROW. A row here is not a record that an
407	 * event occurred — LoginAttempt has no outcome column, nothing reads it but this
408	 * file, and nothing in the product or the admin surfaces it. It is one unit of
409	 * budget that has been spent. Handing the unit back therefore means removing the
410	 * row: the table is a counter, and the honest way to decrement a counter made of
411	 * rows is to delete one. A "negative" marker would mean the count query stops
412	 * being `count(*)` over an index range and becomes a signed sum, which is
413	 * strictly slower, and it would leave rows that outlive their own window and
414	 * still change a verdict. If this table ever needs to double as an audit log,
415	 * that is a different table with a different retention answer, not a sign bit
416	 * bolted onto this one.
417	 *
418	 * WHICH row: the newest for the key, which is what the in-memory predecessor did
419	 * (`hits.pop()`). It is not necessarily the row this very request inserted — a
420	 * concurrent attempt from the same IP may have landed in between — but the
421	 * effect on every window that contains both is identical, and picking the newest
422	 * is the conservative choice, since giving back an older hit would extend the
423	 * bucket's memory rather than shorten it.
424	 */
425	function refund(store: Store, key: string): void {
426	  const hits = store.hits.get(key);
427	  const hit = hits?.pop();
428	  if (!hits || !hit) return;
429	  if (hits.length === 0) store.hits.delete(key);
430	
431	  tombstones.set(hit.id, Date.now() + TOMBSTONE_MS);
432	  enqueueWrite(() => db.loginAttempt.deleteMany({ where: { id: hit.id } }));
433	}

435	/**
436	 * Empty a bucket outright: the account half of a successful login.
437	 *
438	 * Deletes by `(scope, key)` rather than by the ids this process happens to know,
439	 * so guesses recorded against the same account by another process — or before a
440	 * restart — go too. Bounded to rows that existed at the moment of success, so a
441	 * guess arriving during the delete is still counted.
442	 */
443	function clearBucket(store: Store, key: string): void {
444	  const at = Date.now();
445	  store.hits.delete(key);
446	  cleared.set(bucketId(store.scope, key), at);
447	
448	  const scope = store.scope;
449	  enqueueWrite(() =>
450	    db.loginAttempt.deleteMany({ where: { scope, key, createdAt: { lte: new Date(at) } } }),

454	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
455	// Reconcile: rebuild the in-process index from LoginAttempt

458	const RECONCILE_MS = 10_000;

460	/**

lifetime event count on the admin user page. One reader is genuinely affected
and is recorded as a known gap in §6 below: `scanSitePublished` in
`lib/notifications/scan.ts` counts `project.published` events **over all time**
to decide whether a publish is a first publish.

**Form submissions — 365 days, and 30 days if flagged as spam.**
This is the only rule that deletes something a person is waiting to read, so
the number was chosen against readers rather than against disk. Kodely holds
the **only copy**: the owner notification in `lib/site-forms.ts` is
fire-and-forget, is skipped once a project exceeds `EMAIL_MAX_PER_HOUR`, and is
never sent at all for a flagged row. The dashboard shows the newest 200 per
project, so no age-based rule changes what is on screen; the abuse throttles
read a 24-hour window, so any period beyond a day leaves them intact. A year is
the shortest period that still covers the real way a small business reaches
back into a contact inbox ("we heard from them last spring"), and it is a clean
commitment for data belonging to a third party who never had an account here.

The 30-day period for spam is the deliberate asymmetry. The schema keeps
flagged rows rather than dropping them for two stated reasons, and 30 days is
what each actually needs: a false positive is only *recoverable* while the
enquiry still matters to the person who sent it, and a false-positive *rate*
needs a sample and a denominator, not an archive — and a recent sample measures
today's rules rather than last winter's. Spam is also the one class here whose
volume is chosen by the attacker and the one class no product surface delivers:
flagged rows are never emailed and never counted in the unread badge.

**Admin audit — 180 days for reads, permanent for writes.**
An audit log with a short retention defeats itself; one with no retention
becomes a permanent record of which operator opened which customer's account,
which is the second data-protection problem `lib/admin-audit.ts` explicitly
warns against in its own header. So the log is split along the `read`/`write`
classification that file **already declares** in `ADMIN_ACTION_INFO`, rather
than along a list invented here — which means a newly declared write action is
protected the moment it exists, and any action name not in that vocabulary is
left alone.

All of the volume is on the read side: one short browsing session measured
**144 rows**, because `site.viewed` is written on every render of the site
detail page, back button included. 180 days is sized to the question a read row
answers — "who looked at this account, and when" — which is asked when a
customer complains, when a supervisory authority asks, or when an operator's
credentials are suspected. Those arrive within weeks or months of the access,
not years, and six months spans two quarterly reviews with room for a late
complaint. Beyond that the row has stopped being oversight.

**`ProjectFile`, `Message`, `Project`.** The user's actual work. Deleted when
the user deletes the project or the account, never on a timer.

**`EmailLog` — never pruned on a timer. The safe retention here is "never".**
This is the one table where deleting a row causes a **wrong action** rather
than a missing statistic. The row *is* the claim: the unique
`(kind, dedupeKey)` is what makes a transactional send exactly-once, so
removing a row re-arms that send. `dedupeKey` is the id of the thing that
triggered the mail — a ledger row, a build, a project — deliberately **not** a
timestamp, which is what makes the guarantee independent of scheduling and also
means a claim never expires. There is therefore no age at which dropping one is
safe.

The concrete duplicate-send path is `site_published`, whose key is a project
id. A republish is held back from re-mailing by a lifetime count of
`project.published` events in `lib/notifications/scan.ts` — a count the 400-day
event rule eventually empties — which leaves this row as the last thing between
a republish and a second email. It is also reader-facing: the account export
returns it as `emailsSent`. And it is tiny.

Stated honestly: **nothing writes this table today.** `lib/notifications/send.ts`
dedupes in a process-local `Map` that resets on deploy, so the durable guard is
declared in the schema and not yet wired up. That makes this exactly the wrong
moment to also put it on a timer. Its lifecycle is per person, not per clock —
account erasure deletes a user's rows (`app/api/account/_deletion.ts`).

**`AdminAuditLog` rows whose action is a `write`.** For one action the log is
not a record of the change, it is the *only* record: takedown is not a column
anywhere, so `app/admin/sites/page.tsx` reconstructs which sites were taken
down by grouping `site.taken_down` rows. Pruning them would silently
un-take-down sites in the registry view. Writes are also rare and small — a
takedown, a flag flip, a support note — so keeping them forever costs nothing.

**`ModerationFinding` rows with `reviewedAt` still null.** Ageing one out would
mean discarding an abuse report *before anybody read it*, and removing the flag
that says the site needs looking at. A retention job silently emptying a review
queue is the worst failure available to this job. The growth this leaves
unbounded is bounded by doing the reviews; once reviewed, the 400-day rule takes
them.

---

## 4. Data with a period this job does not enforce

**`LoginAttempt` — about 25 hours, pruned by `lib/rate-limit.ts`.**

The rows are the pre-auth rate limiter's counter: one per consumed attempt,
keyed by a client IP or a salted digest of an email address, never a plaintext
address. `lib/rate-limit.ts` prunes anything older than its longest rule window
plus an hour of slack, batched, on its own reconcile timer (every 10 minutes).

That file argues at length that the rule does not belong in `lib/retention.ts`,
and **the argument is correct**. Every rule in this policy answers "how long
should we keep data that still means something", and each one has a reader
behind it. A `LoginAttempt` past the longest window means nothing to anybody:
no query reaches it, no verdict changes because of it, and the only file that
touches the table is the limiter itself — verified, every `db.loginAttempt`
call site is in `lib/rate-limit.ts`. It is spent counter state, and sweeping it
is part of operating the counter.

Two further reasons not to move it, both stronger than the tidiness argument
for moving it. Correctness would become a scheduling problem: nothing runs this
job yet, so a table on the login path would grow unbounded until a cron entry
exists. And a **second** pruner would be actively unsafe — two cutoffs racing,
with the shorter one winning, and a cutoff shorter than the limiter's longest
window deletes rows still inside a live rule window, handing an attacker back
guesses they have already spent. Duplicating the prune is worse than either
choice.

What *was* missing is a stated period, because a privacy policy has to say how
long an IP address is kept and "something else deletes it" is a different
sentence from "we do not delete it". So the period is recorded in
`PRUNED_ELSEWHERE` in `lib/retention.ts` and printed by the runner on every
run, without the job pretending to own it.

## 6. Known gaps

**1. A republish can be congratulated twice.** `scanSitePublished` in
`lib/notifications/scan.ts` decides whether a publish is a *first* publish by
counting `project.published` events for that project **over all time**, and
treating `> 1` as a republish. That count is a correctness guard, and the
400-day event rule empties it: a project first published more than 400 days ago
and republished today counts 1, and is mailed "your site is live" a second
time. The comment on that function — that events outlive anything it looks back
at — is true of the 15-minute slot it scans and not true of this count.

and the backstop is already in the schema: `EmailLog`'s unique
`(kind, dedupeKey)` makes a second `site_published` for the same project
impossible — once something writes `EmailLog`, which nothing does yet. Note the
direction: shortening the event window makes this *more* likely, not less. The
fix is either to bound that count to the project's own lifetime window, or to
wire the `EmailLog` insert that `lib/notifications/send.ts` currently replaces
with an in-process `Map`. Both are outside this file.
